tagline: Where the Sahara meets the Mediterranean
overview:
Tunisia is the northernmost country in Africa, a wedge of land on the Mediterranean between Algeria and Libya. It is about the size of Wisconsin, the smallest country in North Africa, yet it packs in beaches, olive groves, Roman ruins and Sahara dunes. Sicily lies only about 150 kilometers across the water, and for thousands of years that short crossing has made Tunisia a meeting point of Africa and Europe. The capital, Tunis, spreads around a lagoon beside the ruins of ancient Carthage.

About 12 million people live in Tunisia. Arabic is the official language, spoken in a distinctive Tunisian dialect, and French is widely used in business and schools; Amazigh, or Berber, survives in a few southern villages. Tunisia is a republic. Olive oil, dates, phosphates and tourism support the economy, and nearly all Tunisian children, girls and boys alike, attend school, one of the highest rates in the region.
landAndNature: Northern Tunisia is green and hilly, with cork oak forests in the Kroumirie range and wheat fields watered by winter rains. The Dorsal, the tail end of the Atlas Mountains, crosses the country to Jebel ech Chambi, its highest point at about 1,544 meters. South of it lie the chotts, vast salt flats that shimmer white and turn into shallow lakes after rain; Chott el Jerid is the largest in the Sahara. Beyond them stretch sand dunes and palm-filled oases at the desert's edge. Flamingos winter in the coastal lagoons, and the island of Djerba is carpeted with olive and date trees.
peopleAndCulture: Couscous, steamed semolina served with vegetables and lamb or fish, is the national dish, often shared from one large platter on Fridays. Harissa, a fiery chili paste, goes on almost everything, and brik, a crisp pastry folded around an egg, is a street favorite. Mint tea with pine nuts follows a meal. Medinas, walled old towns of narrow alleys and shaded courtyards, form the heart of Tunis, Sousse and Kairouan. Music blends Arab malouf with Mediterranean rhythms, and the Carthage festival fills a Roman theater each summer. Soccer is the national sport, and Tunisia has qualified for several World Cups.
history: Phoenician traders founded Carthage near modern Tunis around 814 BC, and it grew into a sea empire that fought Rome in three long wars; the general Hannibal marched war elephants over the Alps before Carthage was destroyed in 146 BC. Rome rebuilt the region as a grain basket, leaving the huge amphitheater at El Jem. Arab armies arrived in the 600s, bringing Islam and founding the city of Kairouan. Ottoman rule followed, and France took control as a protectorate in 1881. Independence came on March 20, 1956, under Habib Bourguiba, who expanded schooling and women's rights. In 2011 mass protests removed the long-serving president and helped set off uprisings across the Arab world.
funFacts: The Roman amphitheater at El Jem could seat around 35,000 people, nearly as many as the Colosseum in Rome.
Scenes from Star Wars were filmed in southern Tunisia, and some of the desert sets still stand near Tozeur.
Tunisia is among the world's leading olive oil producers, with roughly 80 million olive trees.
In Matmata, families built homes by digging deep pits into the ground, staying cool in the Saharan heat.
Carthage was once Rome's greatest rival, and its ruins now sit in a seaside suburb of Tunis.
